question: In 1992, this man was convicted of raping beauty pageant contestant Desiree Washington and served three years of his sentence in an Indiana prison. In February 1990, he suffered one of the biggest upsets in sports history when 42-to-1 underdog Buster Douglas knocked him out in the tenth round in Tokyo. At just 20 years old in November 1986, he knocked out Trevor Berbick to become the youngest heavyweight champion in boxing history. (*) In a June 1997 rematch billed as "The Bite Fight," he was disqualified for biting off part of Evander Holyfield's ear. For 10 points, name this boxer nicknamed "Iron Mike."

This man was knocked out with one second left in the sixth round of his fourth fight against Juan Manuel Marquez in December 2012, a bout later named Fight of the Year. In 2016, he was elected to the Senate of the Philippines after previously serving in its House of Representatives. This boxer forced Oscar De La Hoya to quit on his stool after the eighth round of their December 2008 bout. (*) In May 2015, he lost a unanimous decision to Floyd Mayweather Jr. in a bout billed as the "Fight of the Century." For 10 points, name this Filipino boxer nicknamed "Pacman," the only eight-division world champion in boxing history.

This boxer's promotional entourage and personal brand are known as "The Money Team," reflecting the nickname he adopted after starting his career as "Pretty Boy." He topped Forbes' list of the world's highest-paid athletes multiple times in the early-to-mid 2010s. In August 2017, he came out of retirement to face UFC star Conor McGregor in a boxing crossover bout, winning by tenth-round TKO to improve to 50 wins. (*) In May 2015, he defeated Manny Pacquiao by unanimous decision in a bout billed as the "Fight of the Century." For 10 points, name this boxer who retired with a perfect 50-0 professional record.

In February 2015, this athlete submitted Cat Zingano via armbar just 14 seconds into their UFC 184 title bout, the fastest finish in UFC title-fight history. She won a bronze medal in judo at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, becoming the first American woman to medal in Olympic judo. In November 2012, she became the first female fighter signed to the UFC and its inaugural women's bantamweight champion. (*) Her title reign ended in November 2015 when Holly Holm knocked her out with a head kick at UFC 193. For 10 points, name this MMA pioneer and WWE star known for her armbar submission.

At age ten in 1995, this driver introduced himself to Ron Dennis at an awards ceremony by saying "one day I'd like to race for your team," and McLaren signed him to its young driver program three years later. In his 2007 rookie season, this man stood on the podium in his very first Grand Prix in Australia and finished the year just one point behind Kimi Räikkönen. (*) This driver is recognized as the first Black driver in Formula One history and, unusually for a top F1 driver, has no widely used paddock nickname. In 2021, this man lost the World Championship to Max Verstappen on the final lap of the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix after a contentious late safety-car restart. For 10 points, name this British driver who holds Formula One's all-time records of 106 Grand Prix wins and a share of the record seven world titles.
answer: Lewis Hamilton [or Lewis Carl Davidson Hamilton]

question: This driver made his Formula One debut as a last-minute substitute for the jailed Bertrand Gachot at the 1991 Belgian Grand Prix, driving for Jordan and out-qualifying his veteran teammate Andrea de Cesaris. Because of his brilliant performances in wet conditions, he earned the nickname "Regenmeister," or rain master. At the 2006 Monaco Grand Prix, he parked his car at the Rascasse corner in an attempt to block Fernando Alonso from taking pole position. (*) In the 1997 season finale at Jerez, he attempted to ram Jacques Villeneuve off the track; he retired from the race and was later disqualified from the championship standings for the maneuver. For 10 points, name this German driver who clinched his first title by colliding with Damon Hill at the 1994 Australian Grand Prix and went on to win a joint-record seven World Championships with Benetton and Ferrari.

Before joining McLaren in 1988, this driver began his Formula One career with Toleman and Lotus. At the 1989 Japanese Grand Prix, he collided with his own teammate Alain Prost, then was disqualified for cutting through a chicane escape road to rejoin the race, handing Prost the championship despite this driver crossing the finish line first. (*) At the same circuit the following year, he deliberately rammed Prost, by then driving for Ferrari, at the first corner to clinch the title, an act he admitted a year later had been intentional. He won World Championships in 1988, 1990, and 1991, all with McLaren. For 10 points, name this Brazilian driver who was killed on May 1, 1994, when his car struck a concrete wall at the Tamburello corner during the San Marino Grand Prix at Imola, a day after Roland Ratzenberger died in qualifying.
answer: Ayrton Senna [or Ayrton Senna da Silva]

question: This driver was recommended to Hendrick Motorsports by Jeff Gordon after his previous team lost its sponsorship. Paired with crew chief Chad Knaus in the No. 48 car, he won the Daytona 500 in both 2006 and 2013, though Knaus was suspended by NASCAR and missed victory lane after the first of those wins. (*) In 2024, this driver was inducted into the NASCAR Hall of Fame. From 2006 through 2010, he won a record five consecutive NASCAR Cup Series championships. For 10 points, name this driver who tied Richard Petty and Dale Earnhardt's record of seven Cup Series titles, all won behind the wheel of Hendrick Motorsports' No. 48 car.

This golfer was inducted into the World Golf Hall of Fame in 1974, years before the end of his playing career. In 1962, this golfer defeated Arnold Palmer in a playoff at Oakmont Country Club to win the U.S. Open for his first professional victory, at age 22. At age 46, this golfer shot a final-round back-nine 30 to win the 1986 Masters, becoming that tournament's oldest champion and claiming a record sixth green jacket. (*) This golfer amassed 73 PGA Tour victories over his career, third all-time. For 10 points, name this golfer nicknamed the 'Golden Bear,' who holds the record for most men's major championships with 18.
answer: Jack Nicklaus [or Jack William Nicklaus; or the Golden Bear]
answerDisplay: Jack Nicklaus [or Jack William Nicklaus; or the Golden Bear]

question: Despite winning four other major titles, this golfer never captured the PGA Championship during his career. In 1967, this golfer became the first player to surpass $1 million in career PGA Tour earnings. At the 1960 U.S. Open, this golfer erased a seven-stroke deficit entering the final round, firing a front-nine 30 en route to a 65 that beat amateur Jack Nicklaus by two strokes at Cherry Hills. (*) A mix of iced tea and lemonade is named for this golfer, whose fans were nicknamed 'Arnie's Army.' For 10 points, name this golfer, known as 'The King,' who was the first man to win the Masters four times.
answer: Arnold Palmer [or Arnold Daniel Palmer; or the King]

question: In the second round of the 2001 Standard Register Ping, this golfer shot a 13-under-par 59, still the only sub-60 round in LPGA Tour history, and went on to win that event with a record score of 27-under. In 2003, this golfer accepted a sponsor exemption to play in the PGA Tour's Colonial tournament, becoming the first woman to compete in a men's PGA Tour event since Babe Didrikson Zaharias in 1945; she shot 71-74 and missed the cut by four strokes. (*) Later that year, this golfer completed a career Grand Slam by winning the LPGA Championship and the Women's British Open. This Swedish golfer won 72 LPGA Tour titles overall. For 10 points, name this golfer who retired with 10 major championships, one of the most dominant players in women's golf history.

At the 2017 Open Championship, this golfer hit his approach on the 13th hole so far right that he had to play his next shot from the driving range, taking an unplayable lie before making a bogey and sparking a five-under stretch over the final six holes to win at Royal Birkdale. The previous year, this golfer squandered a five-shot lead on the back nine of the Masters, hitting two balls into Rae's Creek for a quadruple-bogey seven at the par-3 12th hole. (*) In 2015, this golfer won the Masters wire-to-wire as a 21-year-old, tying Tiger Woods' 72-hole scoring record of 18-under 270. That same year, he also won the U.S. Open. For 10 points, name this golfer who needs only a PGA Championship victory to complete the career Grand Slam.

After losing a 1991 US Open quarterfinal to Jim Courier, this man's comment that he felt "relieved" the pressure to defend his title was gone drew criticism from Courier and Jimmy Connors. In a 1996 US Open quarterfinal against Alex Corretja, this man vomited on court during a fifth-set tiebreak but recovered to save a match point with a lunge volley and win. (*) This man never won the French Open, with a 1996 semifinal as his best showing there. He won his fifth and final US Open title by beating Andre Agassi in four sets in the 2002 final, the last match of his career. For 10 points, name this American nicknamed "Pistol Pete," who won a men's record 14 Grand Slam singles titles, including a record seven Wimbledon championships, before Roger Federer broke his mark.
answer: Pete Sampras [or Petros Sampras; or Pistol Pete]

question: This woman's father Peter was sentenced to 45 months in prison for tax evasion tied to her early earnings, a case that closed in 1997 only after she personally paid a 1.3-million-Deutsche-mark fine. A disturbed fan named Gunter Parche stabbed this woman's rival Monica Seles in 1993, later claiming he did it to help this woman reclaim the world No. 1 ranking. (*) At the 1988 French Open final, this woman demolished Natasha Zvereva 6-0, 6-0 in just 34 minutes, the most lopsided Grand Slam final of the Open Era. She capped a 1988 calendar-year sweep of all four majors by beating Gabriela Sabatini for Olympic gold in Seoul, completing tennis's first "Golden Slam." For 10 points, name this German woman, later married to Andre Agassi, who won 22 Grand Slam singles titles and remains the only player ever to win each major at least four times.

In his first major final, at the 1990 French Open, this man lost to Andres Gomez and later admitted he had been distracted by fear that his wig would fall off. In 1997, this man failed an ATP drug test for crystal methamphetamine and initially lied in a letter claiming a friend had spiked his drink, a fabrication he confessed to years later in his autobiography. (*) At the 1999 French Open final, this man rallied from two sets down to beat Andrei Medvedev in five sets, completing his career Grand Slam at age 29. He became the first male player to complete a career Golden Slam, having also won Olympic singles gold. For 10 points, name this American nicknamed "the Punisher" for his return of serve, who married Steffi Graf and won eight Grand Slam singles titles.

In August 2025, this player replaced coach Matt Daly with biomechanics specialist Gavin MacMillan, having previously worked with Brad Gilbert from mid-2023 to September 2024. At just 15 years old, this player upset five-time champion Venus Williams in straight sets during her Wimbledon main-draw debut in 2019, becoming the tournament's youngest qualifier ever. (*) In 2025, this player beat Aryna Sabalenka in a three-set French Open final, becoming the first American to win that title since Serena Williams in 2015. Two years earlier, she had also beaten Sabalenka for her first major title, at the 2023 US Open, becoming the first American teenager to win that tournament since Serena Williams in 1999. For 10 points, name this American player, born Cori Gauff, who reached a career-high ranking of No. 2.
answer: Coco Gauff [or Cori Dionne Gauff; prompt on "Coco"]

question: This boxer's professional record stands at 44 wins, 10 losses, 2 draws, and 1 no-contest across 57 bouts. On October 25, 1990, this man dethroned James "Buster" Douglas via third-round knockout to claim the WBA, WBC, and IBF heavyweight titles. He is the only fighter to win the unified heavyweight championship on four separate occasions, holding versions of the WBA, WBC, and IBF belts at various points between 1990 and 2001. (*) In a June 1997 rematch billed as "The Sound and the Fury" and later remembered as "The Bite Fight," this man's opponent was disqualified after biting off part of his ear. For 10 points, name this boxer nicknamed "The Real Deal," whose ear was bitten by Mike Tyson.

This boxer completed a sweep of all four world titles at 160 pounds by stopping Oscar De La Hoya to claim the WBO belt, having already taken the WBC crown from Keith Holmes. In a bout postponed two weeks after being scheduled for September 15, 2001, this man scored a twelfth-round TKO of Felix Trinidad at Madison Square Garden to become the first undisputed middleweight champion since Marvin Hagler. In May 2011, at age 46, this man defeated Jean Pascal to break George Foreman's record as the (*) oldest world champion in boxing history, this time at light heavyweight. He broke his own record twice more, becoming the oldest fighter ever to win a title by beating Tavoris Cloud in 2013, then the oldest boxer to unify major belts in 2014. For 10 points, name this boxer nicknamed "The Executioner."

This boxer's professional record includes three losses and two draws in 68 total bouts, with 39 of his 63 wins coming by knockout. In 2013, this man suffered his first loss, dropping a majority decision to Floyd Mayweather Jr. and surrendering his WBC and Ring magazine light middleweight titles. This man fought a trilogy against Gennady Golovkin that opened with a controversial 2017 draw before he won the second and third meetings by decision. In one of the sport's biggest upsets, this man lost a 2022 unanimous decision to (*) Dmitry Bivol after moving up to light heavyweight to challenge for that title. In 2021, this man became the first boxer in history to become the undisputed super middleweight champion, a feat he repeated as a two-time undisputed champion in 2025. For 10 points, name this Mexican boxing superstar nicknamed for his red hair, born Saúl Álvarez.
answer: Canelo Álvarez [or Saúl Álvarez or Canelo]

question: This fighter was once disqualified for landing illegal elbows against Matt Hamill during a bout on The Ultimate Fighter Finale. In 2015, this man was stripped of his title and removed from the rankings after being arrested on felony hit-and-run charges, then withdrew from a planned 2016 rematch after a positive USADA test he blamed on erectile dysfunction medication. This man's rivalry with Daniel Cormier saw him win both of their light heavyweight title fights, the first by decision and the second by knockout. (*) At UFC 128 in 2011, this man defeated Mauricio "Shogun" Rua to become, at 23, the youngest champion in UFC history, a record he still holds. He later moved up in weight, submitting Ciryl Gane at UFC 285 in March 2023 to claim the vacant heavyweight title, adding to his UFC-record 13 light heavyweight title defenses. For 10 points, name this fighter nicknamed "Bones."

This fighter relocated from Lagos, Nigeria to Auckland, New Zealand at age 21 to train at City Kickboxing gym. Before transitioning to MMA, this man compiled a 75-5 kickboxing record with the promotion Glory, though he twice lost to Alex Pereira, by decision in 2016 and by knockout in 2017. At UFC 236 in 2019, this man defeated Kelvin Gastelum to win the interim (*) middleweight title, then knocked out Robert Whittaker at UFC 243 to unify the belt. His kickboxing rival Alex Pereira later beat him again in MMA, taking his UFC middleweight title by TKO at UFC 281 in 2022. For 10 points, name this fighter nicknamed "The Last Stylebender," a two-time UFC middleweight champion.

This fighter is a two-time Combat Sambo World Champion from Dagestan, Russia, who also holds a black belt in judo. This man became the first Russian to win a UFC title, defending his lightweight championship three times. At UFC 229 in October 2018, this man submitted Conor McGregor by neck crank before leaping out of the cage to attack Dillon Danis, sparking a brawl that led to fines and suspensions. (*) His father and head coach, Abdulmanap, died of COVID-19 complications in July 2020. That October, this man submitted Justin Gaethje by triangle choke at UFC 254, then tearfully announced his retirement with a perfect record. For 10 points, name this fighter nicknamed "The Eagle," who retired undefeated at 29-0.

This driver won a record ten consecutive races and a record 27 races overall during the 1967 season alone. At the 1979 Daytona 500, this man inherited the lead after leaders Cale Yarborough and Donnie Allison crashed each other out on the final lap and then brawled on the infield grass, a spectacle that helped make NASCAR must-see TV. (*) This driver's number 43, sponsored by STP, carried him to a record seven Daytona 500 victories. Statistically the winningest driver in NASCAR history, this man retired in 1992 with 1,184 career starts and a record 200 career wins. For 10 points, name this seven-time NASCAR Cup Series champion nicknamed "The King," father of driver Kyle Petty.

This driver holds NASCAR's all-time win records in both of its top touring series below the Cup level, notching 102 victories in the Xfinity Series and 69 in the Truck Series. Nicknamed "Rowdy," he spent most of his career driving for Joe Gibbs Racing before finishing it at Richard Childress Racing, and he won the 2009 Nationwide Series championship. (*) His older brother Kurt Busch also raced full-time in NASCAR's Cup Series. In May 2026, this driver died at age 41 due to complications from pneumonia and sepsis, just days after racing at Watkins Glen. For 10 points, name this late two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion who won 63 Cup races over his career.

This driver's father Jos Verstappen also competed in Formula One during the 1990s and 2000s. At the 2016 Spanish Grand Prix, this driver became F1's youngest-ever race winner at 18 years and 228 days old, on just his first start for Red Bull Racing. At the 2021 British Grand Prix, this driver was launched into the tire barriers at Copse corner after a high-speed (*) collision with Lewis Hamilton, an impact measured at roughly 51G. Later that season, this driver won his first World Championship over Hamilton in a controversial finish at the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix. For 10 points, name this Dutch driver who won four consecutive Formula One championships from 2021 to 2024 while driving for Red Bull.

This driver's airline, which he founded, suffered a fatal crash in Thailand in 1991. After later serving as team principal of Jaguar's F1 team from 2001 to 2002, this man became non-executive chairman of Mercedes, where he was instrumental in convincing Lewis Hamilton to join the team. This driver lost the 1976 championship by a single point to James Hunt after withdrawing from the rain-soaked season finale in (*) Japan out of safety concerns. Weeks earlier at the Nürburgring, this man's Ferrari had crashed and burst into flames, leaving him with severe burns and lung damage so severe that he was given last rites, yet he returned to racing just six weeks later. For 10 points, name this three-time Formula One World Champion, an Austrian who died in 2019.

This driver is the only person to have won IndyCar races in four different decades, en route to 52 career victories, third all-time. No relative of this driver has won the Indianapolis 500 since his own victory there, a 56-year drought sometimes called a "curse" despite his son Michael and grandson Marco both racing at the Brickyard. (*) This man won the Daytona 500 in 1967 and the Indianapolis 500 in 1969. In 1978, driving for Lotus, this man won six Grand Prix races to capture the Formula One World Championship, becoming just the second American to do so after Phil Hill. For 10 points, name this Italian-American racer, the only driver to win the Indy 500, the Daytona 500, and a Formula One title.

In the 2009 Indianapolis 500, this driver's third-place finish remains the best-ever result by a woman at that race, and she was also the first woman to lead laps there. On April 20, 2008, this driver won the Indy Japan 300 at Twin Ring Motegi, finishing ahead of two-time Indy 500 champion Helio Castroneves and becoming the first woman to win an IndyCar Series race. Sponsored throughout her career by (*) GoDaddy.com, this driver moved to NASCAR and drove for Stewart-Haas Racing. In 2013, this driver became the first woman to win a pole position in the NASCAR Cup Series, qualifying for the Daytona 500 at 196.434 miles per hour and later becoming the first woman to lead a lap in that race. For 10 points, name this pioneering female race car driver who retired from full-time competition in 2018.

In 1969, anti-apartheid protesters threw a drink in this golfer's face at the PGA Championship after he defended segregation in his 1966 book Grand Slam Golf. He later admitted he had been "brainwashed," reversing his earlier defense of his native country's regime. Nicknamed "The Black Knight" for his all-black on-course attire, this man (*) won 24 PGA Tour events and, after turning 50, another 19 titles on the Champions Tour. His victory at the 1965 U.S. Open completed a career Grand Slam, making him the first man from outside the United States to achieve the feat. For 10 points, name this South African golfer who won nine major championships, including three Masters titles.

This golfer collapsed at Madrid's Barajas airport in October 2008 due to a brain tumor that would ultimately claim his life at age 54 in May 2011. Paired with countryman Jose Maria Olazabal, he won 11 of 15 Ryder Cup foursomes and fourball matches together, and he later captained Europe to victory in the 1997 event. At the 1979 Open Championship at Royal Lytham, (*) this golfer famously hit his tee shot into a car park on the 16th hole en route to victory, becoming the youngest champion of the tournament in the 20th century. He added two more Open titles, in 1984 and 1988, plus Masters wins in 1980 and 1983, for five major championships in all. For 10 points, name this Spanish golfing legend.

This golfer was the youngest player ever to qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame but had to wait roughly six months for induction because tour rules required ten years of membership. During her 1978 rookie season, she won five consecutive tournaments, a record that still stands, en route to nine total victories and the season money title. She was the first golfer to win LPGA Rookie of the Year and Player of the Year (*) in the same season, also claiming the Vare Trophy for scoring average that year. She won the LPGA Championship three times, in 1978, 1985, and 1989, for her three major titles. For 10 points, name this American golfer, one of the most beloved figures in LPGA history.

In 2007, at age 12, this golfer became the youngest-ever qualifier for the U.S. Women's Open, a mark later broken by Lucy Li. She won her first major championship at the 2014 Kraft Nabisco Championship. At the 2017 ANA Inspiration, a four-stroke penalty triggered by a TV viewer's phone call-in over a marked ball on the 17th hole cost this golfer the tournament lead; (*) she fell in a playoff to Ryu So-yeon, and the incident led to rule changes banning such call-in penalties. She announced her retirement from professional golf effective after the 2024 season, in which she made her seventh and presumably final Solheim Cup appearance as a Stacy Lewis wildcard pick. For 10 points, name this American golfer, a fixture of the LPGA Tour throughout the 2010s and 2020s.

In January 2017, this golfer shot a record-breaking 11-under 59 at the Sony Open in Hawaii, becoming the youngest player ever to break 60 on the PGA Tour, and his 72-hole total broke the tour's scoring record. He was ranked the World No. 1 golfer for five weeks in May 2018. He is one of only six players in PGA Tour history -- alongside Jack Nicklaus, Tom Watson, and Tiger Woods -- (*) to have won 15 tournaments and two majors before turning 30. In 2022, he rallied from seven strokes back entering the final round to beat Will Zalatoris in a playoff at Southern Hills for his second PGA Championship title. For 10 points, name this American golfer who also won the 2017 PGA Championship at Quail Hollow.

This golfer went 4-0 in the 2017 Walker Cup at the Los Angeles Country Club while playing collegiately at Cal, where he later won the 2019 Pac-12 title. He is the only golfer in history to win a major championship in his tournament debut twice. He won the 2020 PGA Championship at TPC Harding Park, (*) edging Dustin Johnson and Paul Casey by two strokes with a final-round 64. The following year, he captured the 2021 Open Championship at Royal St George's by two strokes over Jordan Spieth, becoming only the second player ever to win both the Open and the PGA Championship before turning 25. For 10 points, name this American golfer known for his precise iron play.

This player's habit of grunting loudly on every shot, paired with her use of two-handed strokes off both wings, made her a distinctive sight on tour. On April 30, 1993, a spectator named Günter Parche stabbed this player in the back during a changeover of her match against Magdalena Maleeva in Hamburg. The attack kept her off tour for over two years, though she returned to win the (*) 1996 Australian Open, her ninth and final major title. In 1990, this player beat Steffi Graf in the French Open final to become, at sixteen, the tournament's youngest-ever champion, and the following year she overtook Graf to become the youngest world number one in tennis history. For 10 points, name this Yugoslav-born American tennis star.

Between 1973 and 1979, this player won 125 consecutive matches on clay courts, a stretch that included seven French Open titles. In 1974, she set a then-record 55-match winning streak, a mark that stood until Martina Navratilova won 74 in a row a decade later. This player and Navratilova met 80 times on tour, including 60 finals, with their (*) 1985 French Open final considered one of the rivalry's finest matches. Nicknamed the 'Ice Maiden' for her on-court composure, she retired with 18 Grand Slam singles titles, an Open Era record when she won her final major at the 1986 French Open. For 10 points, name this American tennis champion known for her rivalry with Martina Navratilova and her dominance on clay courts.

In the 1999 French Open final, this player crossed the net to dispute a line call against her opponent, drawing a point penalty and boos from the crowd, then attempted a stunned underarm serve to save match point in the third set. She lost that final to Steffi Graf and left the court in tears, only returning for the trophy ceremony after her mother (*) convinced her to go back. Nicknamed the 'Swiss Miss,' she won the 1997 Australian Open at sixteen years old, making her the youngest Grand Slam singles champion of the Open Era. That same year she became the youngest world number one in tennis history. For 10 points, name this Swiss player who won five Grand Slam singles titles in the late 1990s.

In August 2024, this player tested positive for trimetazidine in an out-of-competition sample, which she attributed to contaminated melatonin tablets, and she accepted a one-month suspension that November. In 2022, she won six consecutive titles, including at Indian Wells, Miami, and Rome, building a 37-match winning streak that tied Martina Hingis's record before Alizé Cornet (*) ended it in the third round of Wimbledon. That same year, she became the first Polish player ever ranked world number one. She has won the French Open four times, in 2020, 2022, 2023, and 2024, plus the 2022 US Open. For 10 points, name this Polish player who has dominated the French Open with four titles there.

After snatching a towel from a ball person and flashing a middle finger during his third-round win over Feliciano López at the 2019 US Open, this player was fined $9,000 and booed by the crowd for the rest of the tournament. He responded to the boos after a fourth-round win by telling the crowd, 'you give me so much energy to win,' before losing that (*) tournament's final to Rafael Nadal. In February 2022, this player became the ATP's world number one. The previous year, he beat Novak Djokovic in straight sets in the 2021 US Open final, denying Djokovic what would have been the first men's calendar Grand Slam since 1969. For 10 points, name this Russian player known for his counterpunching hard-court game.

In 2022, this man was sentenced to two and a half years in prison for bankruptcy fraud after hiding assets and failing to hand over his own Wimbledon trophies to trustees; he was released and deported to Germany by year's end. From 2013 to 2016, he coached Novak Djokovic to six Grand Slam titles before the pair split. Nicknamed 'Boom Boom' for his powerful serve, he won six (*) Grand Slam singles titles of his own and reached the world number one ranking. In 1985, he beat Kevin Curren in the final to become, at seventeen, the youngest men's singles champion in Wimbledon history, and the first unseeded player and first German to win the title. For 10 points, name this German tennis star.

In the 1981–82 season, this player set the NHL record for goals in a season with 92, a campaign that included an NHL-record 50 goals in his first 39 games. On August 9, 1988, this player was traded from the Edmonton Oilers to the Los Angeles Kings along with Mike Krushelnyski and Marty McSorley, in a deal that sent $15 million cash to Edmonton and became known as hockey's "trade of the century." This player won eight Hart Memorial Trophies as MVP and seven consecutive Art Ross Trophies as the NHL's leading scorer. (*) He centered the Edmonton Oilers dynasty that won four Stanley Cups between 1984 and 1988. For 10 points, name this Canadian center nicknamed "The Great One," the NHL's all-time leader in goals, assists, and points.

This player's knees required more than a dozen surgeries, limiting him to just ten games in 1975–76 before he finished his career with 26 games for the Chicago Black Hawks. In 1979, this player was inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame at age 31, making him the youngest inductee up to that point. This defenseman won a record eight consecutive Norris Trophies and three straight Hart Trophies as MVP, becoming the first blueliner to reach 100 points in a season, with 120 in 1969–70. (*) At forty seconds into overtime of Game 4 of the 1970 Stanley Cup Finals, this player scored the Cup-clinching goal against Glenn Hall and was tripped by Noel Picard immediately after. For 10 points, name this Boston Bruins defenseman whose ensuing photograph flying through the air is hockey's most famous image.

In December 1995, a blowup with rookie head coach Mario Tremblay, who left him in net for nine goals against Detroit, led this player to tell Canadiens president Ronald Corey that he had played his last game in Montreal; he was traded to the Colorado Avalanche four days later. During Game 4 of the 1993 Stanley Cup Finals, this player winked at Los Angeles Kings forward Tomas Sandstrom after robbing him on a scoring chance in overtime. This goaltender won three Conn Smythe Trophies as playoff MVP en route to four Stanley Cup titles, two apiece with Montreal and Colorado. (*) He retired in 2003 holding NHL records for career wins with 551 and games played by a goaltender. For 10 points, name this Hall of Fame netminder credited with popularizing the butterfly style of goaltending.

At the 2024 NHL All-Star Skills competition, this player became the first player in NHL history to win the Fastest Skater event four times, clocking a winning time of 13.408 seconds. This player was named captain of the Edmonton Oilers just before the 2016–17 season, becoming the youngest captain in NHL history at 19 years and 266 days old. In 2022–23, this player swept the Art Ross, Hart, Ted Lindsay, and Maurice Richard Trophies in the same season. (*) He has won the Hart Trophy as MVP three times and the Art Ross Trophy as scoring champion five times. For 10 points, name this Oilers superstar center, selected first overall in the 2015 NHL Entry Draft.

On March 28, 1950, this player fractured his skull and suffered a brain hemorrhage after crashing into the boards, requiring emergency surgery in which doctors drilled into his skull to relieve pressure. During the 1973–74 WHA season, this player came out of retirement to play alongside his sons Mark and Marty on the Houston Aeros. A combination of a goal, an assist, and a fight in the same game is popularly named after this player, who was known for both his scoring touch and his toughness. (*) He made a record 23 NHL All-Star Game appearances and led the Detroit Red Wings to four Stanley Cups in the 1950s. For 10 points, name this right wing nicknamed "Mr. Hockey," who died in 2016 at age 88.

This player grew up playing minor hockey in Cole Harbour, Nova Scotia before being selected first overall by the Colorado Avalanche in the 2013 NHL Entry Draft. In 2014, this player won the Calder Memorial Trophy as top rookie, becoming the youngest player ever to do so. This player helped Colorado defeat the Tampa Bay Lightning in six games to win the 2022 Stanley Cup. (*) In 2024, he won his first Hart Trophy after posting 140 points on 51 goals and 89 assists, drawing congratulatory calls from Sidney Crosby and Wayne Gretzky. For 10 points, name this Nova Scotia-born Colorado Avalanche center.
